clue.text: Express taken in by reporter for magazine

indicators.note: taken in by means absorbed by, so the first word's synonym goes inside the word for the reporter

parts.note: a newsman is a journalist who gathers and reports the news
to express an opinion is to state it

explanation.surface: A journalist working for a periodical has fooled the Express newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital makes Express look like the British daily paper; it is just the verb. 'taken in by' reads as fooled by but is the insertion signal, swallowed by; 'for' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The title is a British weekly of politics and culture, so it is an example of a periodical.

clue.text: Force to be precise

definitions.meaning: as a verb, to demand and obtain something by pressure, as a ruler forces tribute from subjects
as an adjective, strictly accurate and correct in every detail

explanation.surface: Someone is compelled to be accurate.
explanation.walkthrough: Two definitions joined by 'to be'. The first is the verb, as in exacting tribute or revenge; the second is the everyday adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: To extort payment by pressure is one sense, and strictly accurate in every detail is the other.

clue.text: Rock group project a fairly short distance away

parts.note: the Stones is the familiar short name of the Rolling Stones, the British rock band
as a verb, to project a missile is to throw it through the air

explanation.surface: A band's building scheme is going up just around the corner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'project' reads as a noun, the band's venture, but it is the verb. The answer is a possessive, STONE'S THROW; the enumeration (6,5) ignores the apostrophe.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for somewhere nearby, no farther off than a pebble could be lobbed.

clue.text: National front in London snubbed foreign lady

indicators.note: foreign in the sense of strange or unfamiliar, so the letters left over are put in an unfamiliar order
to snub is to ignore or cut someone, so the letter just named is cut from the first word

parts.note: taken as written, before it loses a letter

indicators.note: front in means the letter that stands at the head of the word after it

explanation.surface: A far-right party in the capital has rebuffed a woman from abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: The National Front, a British far-right party, is split in two: 'front in' London is L, 'snubbed' drops it from NATIONAL, and 'foreign' rearranges NATIONA.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's given name, the feminine form of Antony, so one example of a female person.

clue.text: Centres for cheap shavers slash Braun?

indicators.note: centres for means the middle letter of each of the three words that come next

explanation.surface: Outlets selling budget razors cut the price of a well-known German brand.
explanation.walkthrough: Braun reads as the German shaver brand; it is the surname of Hitler's companion, and the question mark flags a definition by example. 'Centres for' takes one middle letter from each of the next three words.
explanation.definitionFit: Hitler's companion bore this forename, so her surname with a question mark points to it by example.

clue.text: Almost shy about value in chairs

indicators.note: about means around, so the shortened word for shy goes round the word for value
almost means not quite all of the word for shy: it stops one letter early

parts.note: shy in the sense of bashful and unassuming is modest
to value something highly is to rate it highly

explanation.surface: Someone is rather bashful about the worth of the seating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chairs' looks like furniture; it is a verb. 'Almost' drops the last letter of the word for shy, leaving MODES, and 'about' wraps that round the word for value; 'in' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means presides over a meeting or debate, keeping the speakers in order.

clue.text: Has to have massages by the sound of it

indicators.note: by the sound of it tells you to say the word for massages and go by ear, not spelling

parts.note: as a verb: a masseur massages a stiff muscle or kneads it

explanation.surface: Someone apparently cannot do without regular rubdowns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'massages' reads as a noun, the thing someone must have; it is a verb, KNEADS. 'by the sound of it' asks for a word that sounds the same.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb synonym: whoever requires something must possess it.

clue.text: Unusual somalian portrait

indicators.note: unusual means out of the ordinary, so the letters of the word after it leave their ordinary order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A striking picture of someone from Somalia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unusual' rearranges the eight letters of 'somalian'; the nationality is there only for its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonardo's painting of a Florentine merchant's wife, hanging in the Louvre, is the most famous example.

clue.text: Represented in cartoons as criminal us group

indicators.note: read as re-presented in: the answer is presented afresh, its letters rearranged, in the two words that follow

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Comic strips depict some Americans as a gang of crooks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Represented in' is the anagram signal, re-presented, working on CARTOONS AS; 'criminal', a common anagram word, here belongs to the definition, where 'us' is US, the United States.
explanation.definitionFit: The name, Italian for our thing, is what the American Mafia calls itself.

clue.text: Perhaps does rush around

indicators.note: around means the word for rush is turned round and read from its last letter to its first

parts.note: a rush is a marsh plant with tall hollow stems, much like a reed

explanation.surface: Maybe someone really does dash about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'does' reads as the verb; it is the plural of doe, a female of the species, and 'Perhaps' marks the example. 'around' turns REED back to front.
explanation.definitionFit: Does are the females of this animal, whose plural is unchanged, so they are one example of it.

clue.text: Criticize article about Greek temple

parts.note: to pan a film or play is to review it harshly
the definite article of English grammar
a lecture on a subject is a lecture about it

explanation.surface: Find fault with a piece of writing concerning an ancient Greek shrine.
explanation.walkthrough: Three pieces in a row with no indicator. The famous one stands in Rome, but the word is Greek: pan, all, and theos, god.
explanation.definitionFit: A shrine dedicated to all the gods, its name built from the Greek for all and god.

clue.text: Ref has abuse once again

indicators.note: to abuse something is to treat it roughly, so the two words before it have their letters knocked about

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The match official is being shouted at yet another time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abuse' is not what the official suffers but an instruction to mistreat the six letters of REF HAS.
explanation.definitionFit: An adverb synonym: to start anew is to begin from scratch a second time.

clue.text: Withdrawing sailor's drawing

parts.note: AB, for able-bodied seaman, is a naval rating; the possessive supplies the S
drawing in the sense of pulling, as a horse draws a cart, is traction

explanation.surface: Someone is taking away a seaman's sketch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drawing' looks like a sketch but means pulling. The apostrophe-s of 'sailor's' is kept as a letter, so the seaman gives ABS.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun it is the act of removing or taking something away, matching the gerund.

clue.text: Order car from Italy

definitions.meaning: a formal decree or authoritative command, from the Latin for let it be done
a make of motor car built in Turin

explanation.surface: Someone buys an Italian motor.
explanation.definitionFit: An authoritative decree is one sense, and the Turin carmaker's products are the other.

clue.text: Game diners in a hurry do when leaving a restaurant?

definitions.meaning: an informal form of cricket in which the batsman must go for a run whenever bat touches ball

definitions.text: diners in a hurry do when leaving a restaurant?
definitions.meaning: rushed customers leave a gratuity for the waiter and then dash for the door

explanation.surface: Plucky customers in a rush hurry out of a bistro.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game diners' reads as plucky customers, but 'Game' stands alone as the first definition; the rest is a playful description of leaving a gratuity and dashing.
explanation.definitionFit: It is casual cricket in which any touch of the bat forces a dash, and rushed customers leave a gratuity then bolt.

clue.text: Politician touring managed pose in passing

indicators.note: touring means travelling round, so the politician goes round the two words that follow

parts.note: a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party
someone who managed a shop ran it
to pose for a painter is to sit for a portrait

explanation.surface: An MP on a tour found a moment for a photo opportunity along the way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in passing' reads as one phrase meaning incidentally, but 'in' is a link and 'passing' alone defines. 'touring' sends the politician, a British Conservative, round the other two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An adjective synonym: something fleeting or short-lived does not last.

clue.text: Communist bands let free

indicators.note: as a verb, to band something is to put a ring round it, so the Communist encircles the word for let

parts.note: a red is a familiar name for a Communist, after the colour of the flag
to let a flat is to lease it to a tenant

explanation.surface: Groups of left-wing militants were allowed to go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bands' reads as groups but is a verb, to ring or encircle. 'let free' splits too: 'let' is the property sense, and 'free' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective it describes a prisoner set at liberty and no longer held.

clue.text: Recorder music left on back street in Paris

parts.note: rap is a style of popular music with rhythmic spoken lyrics
port is the left-hand side of a ship, facing forward

indicators.note: back means the French word for a street is read from its last letter to its first

parts.note: rue is the French word for a street, so what a Parisian calls one

explanation.surface: Sheet music for a woodwind instrument was abandoned in a Parisian alley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recorder' reads as the woodwind instrument; it is a person who records. 'back' belongs with the street, turning RUE into EUR, not with 'back street'; 'on' just joins.
explanation.definitionFit: A person appointed to write up and report the proceedings of a committee or conference.

clue.text: English and Italian leader welcoming a short time in train

indicators.note: welcoming means letting in, so the Italian leader takes the two letters that follow inside

parts.note: Il Duce, Italian for the leader, was the title Mussolini took
short asks for the abbreviation of time, which is t

explanation.surface: Two heads of government greet each other briefly aboard a railway carriage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in train' suggests a railway carriage; 'train' is the verb, to teach, and 'in' a link. 'welcoming' puts A and T inside DUCE, after E.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb synonym: to teach or school someone is to give them instruction.

clue.text: From which one may get bargains in Jerusalem

definitions.text: From which one may get bargains

indicators.note: in says the wanted letters stand together inside the name of the city that follows

explanation.surface: A place in the Holy City where shoppers can pick up cheap goods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in Jerusalem' looks like the location of a market; 'in' is the hidden-word signal and four neighbouring letters of the city's name are the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An event at which shops cut their prices, so shoppers come away with cheap goods.

clue.text: Parent's ticking off two presents

indicators.note: two says the word for the present is written out a second time, one copy after the other

parts.note: the present is the time that is now; the plural matches there being a pair of them

explanation.surface: Mum crosses a couple of gifts off her list.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ticking off' reads as marking a list but is British for a telling-off; 'presents' are not gifts but the present moment, NOW, which 'two' doubles.
explanation.definitionFit: A gentle reproof or soothing rebuke, the sort a mother gives a squabbling child.

clue.text: Cross inside, flyer cut up woodland flower

indicators.note: inside puts the cross within the turned letters of the shortened flyer
up, in a down entry, means the shortened flyer is read from its bottom letter to its top
cut means the word for a flyer is cut short, losing its last letter

parts.note: a pilot flies an aircraft, so is a flyer
a cross is the shape of the letter X

explanation.surface: Angry indoors, someone tore up a leaflet about a forest plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' and 'flyer' read as angry and a leaflet. 'cut' trims PILOT to PILO, 'up' turns that into OLIP in this down entry, and 'inside' slots X in.
explanation.definitionFit: A yellow primula of damp woods, a cousin of the cowslip and the primrose.

clue.text: America's calumnies in conflict I disregarded

indicators.note: in conflict means at odds, so the letters that remain battle their way into a new order
disregarded means ignored, so the letter named just before it is left out of the long word

parts.note: taken as written, before it loses a letter

explanation.surface: The US spread slanders in wartime, and the speaker took no notice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I disregarded' is not the speaker ignoring slander: 'disregarded' drops the I from CALUMNIES, and 'in conflict' rearranges CALUMNES. The 's just means is.
explanation.definitionFit: The white-bearded figure in a star-spangled top hat personifies the United States and its government.

clue.text: Pick needed for some concrete tiles coming up

indicators.note: coming up, in a down entry, means the run of letters is read from the bottom towards the top
some means only part of the two words after it is wanted, a run of neighbouring letters

explanation.surface: A pickaxe is required to lift a few paving slabs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pick' looks like the tool; it means the best, as in the pick of the bunch. 'some' takes ETILE from where 'concrete' meets 'tiles', and 'coming up' turns it over.
explanation.definitionFit: The choicest members of a group, the cream or the best of the bunch.

clue.text: Endless run on pound is about to fade

indicators.note: is about means the two pieces, once joined, are turned about and read from right to left
endless means the word run goes without its end, its last letter

parts.note: taken as written, before it loses its end
lb, from the Latin libra, is the abbreviation for a pound in weight

explanation.surface: A relentless wave of selling sterling is on the point of dying away.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a currency panic, a run on the pound. 'Endless' leaves RU, LB follows, and 'is about' turns RULB round.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb synonym: to become dim and indistinct, as an old photograph or a memory does.

clue.text: Is a bit less shaky

indicators.note: shaky means unsteady, so the four words before it have their letters jolted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Something has steadied slightly.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: 'shaky' rearranges IS A BIT LESS, and whatever becomes a bit less shaky does this.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that steadies grows firmer and wobbles less than before, which is what the whole clue describes.

clue.text: Note broadcast on the radio

indicators.note: on the radio means the word for broadcast is heard, not seen, so only its sound counts

parts.note: to broadcast seed is to scatter it by hand, which is to sow it

explanation.surface: A memo was read out over the airwaves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broadcast' is not a transmission but the older farming sense, scattering seed: SOW. 'on the radio' asks for a word that sounds like it.
explanation.definitionFit: The fifth degree of the sol-fa scale, also spelt so or sol, as in doh-ray-me.

clue.text: Nick's given pasta seconds around Italy? Not by these!

indicators.note: given says the word for nick has the rest handed to it, so the pasta piece follows straight after

parts.note: to nick is British slang for to steal, as is to pinch; the apostrophe-s stands for has

indicators.note: around means the pasta with its extra letter goes round the letter for Italy

parts.note: penne is pasta in short tubes cut on the slant
I is the international vehicle registration letter for Italy
s is the abbreviation for seconds, as in timings

explanation.surface: A man called Nick is served second helpings of pasta all over Italy, though not by the stingy.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is generous second helpings; the last three words name people who would never serve them. 'given' attaches the pasta to the word for nick, and 'around' wraps that pasta, with its abbreviation for seconds, round Italy's letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Misers grudge every coin, so nobody would get extra helpings from them, which is the clue's closing joke.
